intro:
The best weed eater for most yards is the EGO Power+ ST1521S: a 56-volt brushless trimmer with a 15-inch swath, 0.095-inch line and a Powerload head that winds new line onto the spool at the push of a button. It does what a small gas trimmer did, starts instantly and needs no fuel can.

Gas still wins on big rural properties and in thick, woody growth, and a light 20-volt trimmer is all a townhouse lot needs. Below are seven picks matched to yard size and power source, followed by the questions buyers ask most: swath and line size, the easiest heads to reload, batteries and runtime, brands, technique and upkeep.
quickAnswer: Buy the EGO ST1521S for most suburban yards. Choose the Ryobi ONE+ HP 18V brushless if you already own Ryobi batteries, the Stihl FS 56 RC-E for gas power with easy starting, or the Greenworks Pro 80V 16-inch for half-acre to one-acre lots. For small yards, the Worx WG163 and BLACK+DECKER LSTE525 are light trimmer-edgers.

Then match swath and line to the growth. A 12-inch swath with thin line tidies a well-kept lot; a 15- to 16-inch swath with 0.080- to 0.095-inch line handles overgrown edges.

sections.heading: The 7 Best Weed Eaters in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
Picks are drawn from maker specifications, including swath, line diameter, voltage and engine size, plus the attachments each platform supports and recurring themes in owner reviews. They are ranked on how well each fits a realistic yard and budget.

### Best Overall: EGO Power+ ST1521S Powerload

The ST1521S is the battery trimmer that talked many gas owners into switching. It runs on EGO's 56-volt platform with a brushless motor, cuts a 15-inch swath and uses 0.095-inch line, thick enough for tall grass along a fence and overgrown bed edges. A variable-speed trigger and high and low settings let you trade power for runtime.

Its standout feature is Powerload. Press a button and the head winds fresh line onto the spool itself; you just feed a length through the head instead of hand-winding a spool on the driveway. Owners commonly say that alone is worth the price. The long shaft suits taller users, and the battery at the rear balances the head well.

The downsides are weight once a large battery is fitted, a Powerload head that costs more to replace than a basic bump head, and the commitment to EGO's batteries and chargers. If you already own an EGO mower or blower, it is an easy call.

**Pros:** push-button line winding; 15-inch swath and 0.095-inch line; brushless with variable speed; shares a big EGO battery lineup.

**Cons:** heavier than 20V trimmers with a big pack; pricier replacement head; locks you into EGO.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=EGO+ST1521S&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Value: Ryobi ONE+ HP 18V Brushless

Ryobi's ONE+ HP brushless trimmer runs on the same 18-volt batteries as hundreds of Ryobi drills, saws and yard tools, which is why it sells so well. If you already have a couple of ONE+ packs, the bare tool costs little. The brushless motor is a clear step up from Ryobi's older brushed trimmers, and the adjustable cutting width lets you run a narrow path for longer runtime or a wide one for speed.

It uses a standard bump-feed head with common 0.080-inch line, so refills are cheap and sold everywhere. It suits small and mid-size suburban lots: edging a driveway and cleaning up along beds and fences. On thick weeds or a long overgrown fence row, 18 volts runs out of punch before a 56-volt or gas machine, and a 4Ah or larger battery makes a noticeable difference.

**Pros:** shares batteries with a huge Ryobi range; brushless with adjustable width; inexpensive line; light for long edging sessions.

**Cons:** less power in heavy growth; runtime depends on battery size; bump head needs hand rewinding.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ryobi+ONE%2B+HP+18V+brushless+string+trimmer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Gas: Stihl FS 56 RC-E

The FS 56 RC-E is a dealer-sold Stihl that does what gas trimmers do best: runs as long as you have fuel, with steady power in thick, wet or woody growth. Its 27.2cc two-stroke engine runs on a 50:1 fuel and oil mix, and Stihl's Easy2Start system cuts the pull force needed to start it, which matters on a tool you might start ten times a weekend.

The straight shaft keeps the head well out front for reaching under shrubs and decks. Buying through a Stihl dealer means the tool arrives assembled and explained, and repairs stay local. The downsides are shared by every gas trimmer: noise that calls for hearing protection, exhaust, fuel storage and seasonal upkeep such as air filter cleaning and spark plug changes. Use ethanol-free premix or fresh fuel with stabilizer to keep the carburetor clean.

**Pros:** unlimited runtime with fuel; Easy2Start; straight shaft for reach; local dealer service.

**Cons:** loud; mixed fuel and seasonal maintenance; more weight and vibration than battery models.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Stihl+FS+56+RC-E&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Big Yards: Greenworks Pro 80V 16-Inch

Greenworks' 80-volt platform is built around high-output yard tools, and its 16-inch trimmer is among the widest-cutting battery trimmers sold to homeowners. The brushless motor and wide swath clear long fence lines and roadside ditches faster than a narrower 18- or 20-volt model, which makes half-acre to one-acre owners its natural audience.

It uses a bump-feed head with heavier line than entry-level trimmers. Greenworks sells the same 80V battery across mowers, blowers, chainsaws and riding equipment, so a property owner can run nearly everything on one battery family. Expect more weight than a compact trimmer and a larger upfront cost if you are starting the platform from scratch. Some versions come with an attachment-capable shaft, so check the model if you want to add an edger later.

**Pros:** 16-inch swath; brushless on a high-voltage platform; one battery for many tools; strong in tall grass.

**Cons:** heavy next to 20V trimmers; big starter-kit cost; fewer service points than gas dealers.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Greenworks+Pro+80V+16+inch+string+trimmer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Lightweight: Worx WG163 GT 3.0 20V

The WG163 is built for small yards and people who dislike heavy tools. It cuts a 12-inch path, is light enough to hold out at arm's length for a whole session, and converts from trimmer to wheeled edger by rotating the head and folding down a small guide wheel. Its Command Feed button advances line on demand, so there is no bumping the head on the ground.

Kits usually include two 20-volt batteries, which makes sense for a tool with modest runtime per pack. For a townhouse lot or a small suburban yard with a short driveway, it handles routine edging and trimming easily. It is not built for neglected fence rows, thick weeds or woody stems, and its 0.065-inch line wears quickly against concrete.

**Pros:** very light; converts to an edger in seconds; push-button line feed; two batteries in most kits.

**Cons:** thin line struggles in thick weeds; 12-inch swath is slow on bigger lots; not for brush.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Worx+WG163+GT+3.0&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Multi-Tool: Husqvarna 128LD

The 128LD is a gas trimmer with a split shaft that accepts Husqvarna attachments, so one engine can run a trimmer head, an edger, a pole saw or a cultivator. It uses a 28cc two-stroke engine on a 50:1 mix and a straight shaft, with a primer bulb and a reduced-effort starting system to make pulls easier.

If you want a gas trimmer plus an occasional edger or pole saw without buying separate engines, the value is real. As a pure trimmer it is competent rather than exceptional, with typical consumer gas noise and vibration, and the shaft coupling should be kept clean and tight. It suits mid-size and larger properties where battery runtime would be a limit.

**Pros:** detachable shaft runs several attachments; steady 28cc power; straight shaft; parts and service widely available.

**Cons:** gas noise and vibration; mixed fuel and upkeep; attachments cost extra.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Husqvarna+128LD&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget: BLACK+DECKER LSTE525 20V MAX

The LSTE525 is one of the cheapest ways into a cordless trimmer that also edges. It runs on BLACK+DECKER 20V MAX batteries, cuts a 12-inch swath and rotates into an edger with a wheel guide. An automatic feed system advances line without bumping, and a two-speed switch lets you choose power or runtime.

For a small yard with a short walk, it is enough tool, and it is light enough for occasional users. The limits show quickly: the thin line and modest motor bog down in thick or wet weeds, runtime on the included battery is short, and the auto-feed spool can tangle if line is wound loosely. If your yard is a quarter acre or less and you mostly trim around beds and a walkway, it is a fair buy.

**Pros:** low cost for a trimmer-edger; two-speed control; automatic feed; light.

**Cons:** short runtime; struggles in thick weeds; spool tangles if wound loosely.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=BLACK%2BDECKER+LSTE525&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: Battery, Gas or Corded: Which Weed Eater Should You Buy?
sections.body:
Buy battery for most yards under half an acre, gas for large rural properties and regular brush, and corded only for a tiny yard beside an outdoor outlet. The power source matters more than any other spec, and it should follow your property, not habit.

| Power | Best for | Strength | Drawback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Battery 18-24V | Small lots, edging | Light, cheap if you own the platform | Limited power and runtime |
| Battery 40-80V | Most suburban yards | Near-gas power, quiet, instant start | Higher kit cost, battery weight |
| Gas two-stroke | Large and rural properties | Unlimited runtime, torque in brush | Noise, fumes, fuel and upkeep |
| Corded electric | Tiny yards near an outlet | Lowest cost, no batteries | Cord management, short reach |

### Why battery is the default

A battery trimmer starts instantly and runs quietly enough that you can edge at eight in the morning without waking the street. The better 40- to 80-volt models cut wide swaths with thick line, and one charged battery covers a typical suburban trim and edge.

### When gas still wins

Past half an acre, or anywhere with long fence lines, ditches and woody edges, a gas trimmer is the simpler choice because a fuel can refills it in seconds. Gas also wins if you clear thick weeds every week.

### Think about your other tools

A trimmer is usually the second or third tool on a battery platform after a mower or blower, and shared batteries make each new tool cheaper. If you own an EGO mower or a Ryobi drill kit, weigh that heavily. Our [leaf vacuum guide](/best-leaf-vacuum/) and [self-propelled mower picks](/best-self-propelled-lawn-mower/) include models on the same platforms.

sections.heading: What Cutting Swath and Line Size Do You Need?
sections.body:
Pick a 12-inch swath for a small, tidy lot, 15 inches for most suburban yards and 16 to 17 inches for big properties. Use 0.065-inch line for light trimming, 0.080-inch for general homeowner work and 0.095-inch for overgrown edges.

### Swath

The swath is the diameter of the circle the spinning line cuts. A wider swath clears ground faster along fences and open edges, but it draws more power, so a wide swath on a weak motor drains batteries fast and bogs down in thick grass. Match the swath to the power behind it.

### Line diameter

Thin 0.065-inch line is light and fine for soft grass around beds, but it snaps against concrete and stalls in thick weeds. About 0.080 inches is the common middle ground. Heavier 0.095-inch line cuts tall grass and tough weeds without shredding and lasts longer against curbs and posts. Always use the diameter your head is designed for; oversized line overloads the motor and jams the spool.

### Line shape

Round line is cheapest and most durable. Twisted and star-shaped lines cut more cleanly and quietly in grass but can wear faster on hard edges. Square and serrated profiles slice tougher weeds. None of them turn a 20-volt trimmer into a brush cutter.

### When you need a blade

For saplings, blackberry canes or woody brush, a string trimmer is the wrong tool. Use a gas trimmer or high-voltage battery power head that the maker approves for a metal brush blade, with the handlebar, harness and blade guard it specifies.

sections.heading: What Is the Easiest Weed Eater to Load New Line In?
sections.body:
The EGO ST1521S is the easiest here to reload, because its Powerload head winds the line onto the spool for you at the push of a button. Reloading a spool by hand is the most common complaint about trimmers, so the line system deserves real weight in your choice.

### The four common head types

- **Bump feed** releases line when you tap the head on the ground. It is simple, cheap and reliable once you learn the rhythm, but the spool must be rewound by hand. The Ryobi and Greenworks picks use this style.
- **Automatic feed** advances line on its own as it wears. It is convenient but can waste line or tangle if wound loosely, as owners of the BLACK+DECKER LSTE525 sometimes report.
- **Push-button feed**, such as Worx Command Feed, releases line on demand without bumping.
- **Auto-winding heads** such as EGO Powerload remove the rewinding job entirely.

### Winding a bump head without tangles

Wind tightly and evenly in the direction of the arrow on the spool, keep the two lines from crossing, and use only the diameter printed on the head. Line that will not feed was usually wound loosely or crossed over itself. Old nylon line goes brittle as it dries out, and some owners soak a spool in water overnight before winding it.

sections.heading: How Much Voltage and Runtime Does a Battery Weed Eater Need?
sections.body:
For a typical suburban yard, a 40- to 56-volt trimmer with one mid-size battery covers a full trim and edge. For long fence lines or a half-acre and up, plan on 56 to 80 volts and a second battery.

### Volts and amp-hours

Voltage sets the power class, and amp-hours set how long a battery lasts. A 56- or 80-volt platform can drive a wider swath with thicker line. A higher amp-hour pack on the same platform runs longer but adds weight. Brushless motors pull more work from the same battery, which is why nearly every serious battery trimmer now uses one.

### Read runtime claims carefully

Box runtimes assume light grass, the low speed setting and a full-size battery. Thick growth on high speed drains packs much faster. Owning two batteries and swapping halfway through is the most practical fix.

### Weigh it with the battery in

A high-capacity battery can add two to four pounds, and that weight sits at the far end from the head, changing the balance. Pick the trimmer up with the battery you will actually use before you buy.

### Battery care

Store packs indoors at moderate temperatures, partly charged over winter, and let a hot battery cool before charging. Use only the maker's charger, and register the tool so the battery warranty is easy to claim.

sections.heading: What Are the Most Popular Brands of Weed Eaters?
sections.body:
The most popular weed eater brands are EGO, Ryobi, Greenworks, Worx and BLACK+DECKER on the battery side, and Stihl and Husqvarna on the gas side. DeWalt and Milwaukee also sell broad outdoor battery lines. The best brand for you is usually the one whose batteries you already own.

### Battery platforms

- **EGO** 56V: premium yard platform with mowers, blowers and the Powerload trimmer.
- **Ryobi** ONE+ 18V and 40V: the widest tool range, sold at Home Depot.
- **Greenworks** 80V Pro: high-output tools up to riding equipment.
- **Worx** 20V Power Share: light tools for small yards.
- **BLACK+DECKER** 20V MAX: budget tools for occasional use.

### Gas brands

Stihl sells through dealers who assemble, fuel and service the tool, while Husqvarna is sold through dealers and big retailers with wide parts availability. Both have long histories with professional crews, which is why many owners call them the highest quality gas weed eaters.

### Picking a platform

Batteries do not swap between brands without adapters that can void warranties, so pick a platform that offers the other tools you expect to buy, such as a blower or chainsaw. If you are also shopping for a mower, our [gas lawn mower guide](/best-gas-lawn-mowers/) and [zero-turn mower picks](/best-zero-turn-mower/) cover the bigger machines.

sections.heading: How Do You Trim and Edge With a Weed Eater?
sections.body:
Let the tip of the line do the cutting, keep the head a few inches above the ground, and walk at a steady pace. Most ragged results come from burying the head in the grass.

### Trimming

Tilt the head slightly and swing it in an even arc, taking the top of tall grass first and working down rather than plowing in at ground level. The tip moves fastest and cuts best; pushing the whole line into the grass slows it and wears it out.

### Know your spin direction

Most trimmers spin counterclockwise viewed from above, which throws clippings to the right. Work so clippings land on the lawn or the area you already cut, not on a clean driveway or into a flower bed. Along a fence or wall, approach so the line spins away from the surface.

### Edging

Rotate the trimmer so the head spins vertically, line it up with the driveway or walk, and move slowly. A guide wheel, like the one on the Worx WG163 and BLACK+DECKER LSTE525, keeps the cut straight. The first edge of the season is the hardest; edging every couple of weeks keeps a crisp line with little effort.

### Around trees

Keep the line off trunks. Repeated strikes strip bark and can girdle and kill a young tree. A mulch ring around each tree removes the need to trim there at all. Afterward, blow clippings off hard surfaces, and if you wash the driveway, a [pressure washer surface cleaner](/best-surface-cleaner-for-pressure-washer/) leaves the slab even.

sections.heading: How Do You Maintain a Weed Eater?
sections.body:
Keep the head clean, use fresh line of the right size, and on gas models use fresh mixed fuel and service the filter and plug every season. Most trimmer trouble starts in the head or the carburetor.

### The head

Grass and dirt pack around the spool and eyelets, stopping line from feeding and adding vibration. Pop the cover off every few sessions and brush it out. Check the line-cutting blade on the guard, and replace the guard if it is cracked. On battery models, wipe clippings off the motor vents so the motor can cool.

### Gas engines

Use the ratio printed on the tool, usually 50:1 for modern two-strokes, with oil made for air-cooled two-stroke engines. Fuel that sits more than about a month can varnish the carburetor, so add stabilizer or buy ethanol-free premix. Clean or replace the air filter regularly and check the spark plug each season.

### End of season

For battery tools, clean the head, store the trimmer indoors and store the pack partly charged. For gas, empty or stabilize the tank, clean the filter and hang the trimmer rather than resting it on the head. Maintained this way, a good trimmer lasts many seasons.

sections.heading: What Safety Gear Do You Need for a Weed Eater?
sections.body:
Wear impact-rated safety glasses every time, plus long pants, closed shoes and, with gas, hearing protection. A trimmer head spinning at several thousand rpm throws stones, glass and twigs hard enough to injure eyes and crack windows.

### Eyes and ears

Use glasses or goggles that meet the ANSI Z87.1 impact standard, even for a two-minute touch-up; ordinary prescription glasses are not a substitute. A face shield over glasses helps near gravel. Gas trimmers are loud enough at the operator's ear that earplugs or muffs are a sensible default.

### Body and hands

Wear long pants and sturdy closed shoes or boots, never shorts and sandals. Gloves reduce vibration fatigue and protect your hands when you clear the head.

### Bystanders

Many trimmer manuals specify a hazard zone of about 50 feet for people and pets. Stop the tool if anyone approaches, and shield or avoid parked cars and windows. Walk the area first and pick up stones, wire and toys.

### Clearing jams

Stop the engine or motor before touching the head, and remove the battery on cordless models. Keep the guard installed: it deflects debris and holds the blade that trims line to length. Refuel gas models with the engine cool and away from where you will start it.

mistakes.title: Buying too small a trimmer for the yard
mistakes.body: A light 20-volt trimmer is fine on a townhouse lot and miserable on a half-acre with fence rows. If you finish every session with a dead battery and half the job left, the tool is undersized. Match swath and voltage to the property, or buy a second battery.

mistakes.title: Using the wrong line diameter
mistakes.body: Line thicker than the head is built for overloads the motor and jams the spool, while line that is too thin snaps constantly. The correct size is printed on the head or in the manual. Stick to it, and replace old, brittle line.

mistakes.title: Trimming without eye protection
mistakes.body: Spinning line throws stones and debris at high speed, and trimmer eye injuries are common. Wear impact-rated glasses or goggles every time, however small the job, and add hearing protection with gas.

mistakes.title: Scalping trees and fence posts
mistakes.body: Running the line into a trunk strips bark and can kill young trees, while hitting posts and siding shreds line and leaves marks. Mulch rings around trees and slow passes near structures save the tree, the line and your time.

mistakes.title: Storing a gas trimmer with old fuel
mistakes.body: Fuel left in the tank over winter varnishes the carburetor and causes hard starts in spring. Run the tank dry or add stabilizer before storage, or use ethanol-free premix, and start the season with fresh fuel at the ratio on the tool.

faqs.q: How long does a weed eater battery last per charge?

A mid-size pack on a quality trimmer typically covers one suburban trim and edge, while thick weeds on high speed drain it much faster. bottomLine: The EGO Power+ ST1521S is the weed eater to buy for most yards: 56 volts, a 15-inch swath, 0.095-inch line and a Powerload head that ends hand-winding for good. Pick the Ryobi ONE+ HP if you already own Ryobi batteries, the Stihl FS 56 RC-E or Husqvarna 128LD for gas power on large properties, the Greenworks Pro 80V for half-acre to one-acre lots, and the Worx WG163 or BLACK+DECKER LSTE525 for small, tidy yards.
